actionable: Airtable record-create steps drop the Rule 6 `headers` parameter whenever they are not a Rule 5 fan-out (srw-02 3/3, ctfm-03 2/3); the cause is Rule 6's row-positional scoping vs. the Airtable `fields` dict payload, NOT the missing_parameters interaction.
problem: Every Airtable record-create step that is not a Rule 5 fan-out now omits the Rule 6 `headers` parameter — srw-02 on 3/3 repeated runs and ctfm-03 on 2/3, against a Phase-3 baseline in which both carried it — so 2 of the 24 eval traces fail the `sheet-header-safety` tier-0 criterion and, at execution time, the single record they write is liable to be consumed as the column-header row and silently lost (tier0_code_checks.py:115-128; planner.py:56).
verdict: The dispatch hypothesis is REFUTED. `headers` loss is NOT conditioned on the step carrying a `missing_parameters` entry, and Rule 2's FINAL CHECK bullet is not the trigger. Four post-optimize row-write steps DO carry a flagged-missing key on the writing step and ALL FOUR keep `headers` (amb-02 s2, srw-01 s1, srw-03 s2, fan-01 s2), while ctfm-03 s1 — which has an EMPTY `missing_parameters` array, so Rule 2's clarification block and its FINAL CHECK loop are never entered at all — DROPS `headers`. The actual discriminator across all six post-optimize row-write steps is the payload SHAPE: an Airtable-native `fields` object (a dict whose keys already are the column names) on a step with no `for_each` loses `headers` 2/2; every `row_data`-shaped payload and every fan-out keeps it 4/4. Rule 6 (planner.py:56) is byte-for-byte UNCHANGED by all four shipped fixes (verified: git diff 0639887..HEAD), so the regression is a shift in prompt COMPETITION, not an edit to Rule 6. Two shifts are jointly responsible. (1) SCOPE: Rule 6 states its applicability purely in positional-row vocabulary — 'writes row(s)', 'alongside the row data', 'the row-data placeholder', 'one row with one cell per field, in the same order as `headers`' — and justifies itself with a strictly positional mechanism ('tools otherwise treat the very first row of data as the column headers'). None of that engages a key-addressed `fields` dict, where there is no ordering and no positional first row. Its two named triggering shapes are both cross-references to OTHER rules (a Rule 5 fan-out, a Rule 3 extraction); srw-02 and ctfm-03 invoke neither. The model is following Rule 6's stated REASONING correctly and its intended LETTER incorrectly. (2) EXEMPLAR TRANSFER: the two fixes added the prompt's only two worked `parameters` objects, and they are app-split. planner.py:33 (28320b1) shows `{"row_data": ..., "headers": [...]}` — Google Sheets, WITH headers, framed exhaustively as 'is exactly'. planner.py:53 (71fb7b1) shows the prompt's ONLY Airtable `parameters` enumeration — 'keep `base_name: "Content Calendar"` in `parameters`' — WITHOUT headers. Post-fix, each app's emitted key set converges on its own exemplar: all three Google Sheets writes keep headers (amb-02's post-fix key set `[row_data, headers]` is a character-for-character copy of the line-33 exemplar), and the Airtable writes shed everything the line-53 exemplar does not name. fan-01 survives only because it is the fan-out shape Rule 6 names explicitly and its `["Title"]` matches Rule 6's own `["Caption"]` single-column instance. The srw-02 seed rationale predicted this exact mechanism in advance: 'the planner is more likely to treat \'record\' as structurally different and drop headers.'

The difference is `for_each`: fan-01 is the Rule 5 fan-out that Rule 6's scope clause names EXPLICITLY as a covered shape, and its single-column `["Title"]` is a direct instance of Rule 6's own `["Caption"]` example. BASELINE (pre-optimize), traces/planner-eval-traces.jsonl — ctfm-03 s1 was `{"base_name": "Sales CRM", "table_name": "Deals", "fields": {...}, "headers": ["Deal Name", "Amount", "Stage"]}` and srw-02 s1 was `{"base_name": ..., "table_name": "Invoices", "record_data": {...}, "headers": [5 columns]}`. secondaryObservations.priority: HIGH — recommend its own finding before the next promotion
secondaryObservations.observation: The over-pruning effect the dispatch brief hypothesised is REAL, but its footprint is destination-identity keys, not `headers`, and it has already caused two clear regressions plus two rule violations that no criterion currently catches. Baseline -> post-optimize: (a) ctfm-01 went from `parameters {database_name: "Bug Tracker", title, properties}` with `missing_parameters: []` to `parameters {title, properties}` with `database_name` FLAGGED MISSING — but the user literally said 'my Notion database called Bug Tracker', so a user-given literal was deleted; (b) msh-03 step 3 went from `{database_name: "Vendor Requests", content}` / no clarification to `{content, title}` with `parent_page_id` flagged — the user said 'my Notion database called Vendor Requests', so again a user-given literal was dropped, AND `parent_page_id` is an opaque internal ID, which planner.py:39 explicitly forbids asking for; (c) amb-01 changed its flagged key from `channel` to `channel_id`, also an opaque ID forbidden by planner.py:39; (d) srw-01 and srw-03 each gained a new `sheet_name` (tab-name) clarification where the baseline asked nothing, though both kept their user-given `spreadsheet_name` literal, so these two are mild over-clarification rather than literal loss. (a) and (b) directly contradict Rule 5's 'any name or value the user literally said belongs in `parameters` as a concrete literal' (planner.py:53) and were the exact risk flagged as untested in diagnose-finding-5-amb02.json's applyInstructions step 6 and in its fourth assumption.
secondaryObservations.possibleContributingCause: Rule 2's FINAL CHECK (planner.py:35) is a purely SUBTRACTIVE last-pass instruction sitting immediately before the schema, with high recency and no counterbalancing 'and confirm every other required field is still present' half. Its closing phrase 'keep only the `missing_parameters` entry' is readable as a minimality directive. Combined with planner.py:34's 'An intentionally incomplete step body plus a `missing_parameters` entry IS the correct, complete output', the prompt now rewards incompleteness in the destination slot, and the model appears to be resolving borderline cases toward flagging-and-omitting. Note this pressure operates on the DESTINATION key class the new bullets enumerate (spreadsheet_name, database_name, table_name, 'Sheet1'/'Orders'/'General'/'#general'), which is why it does not explain the `headers` loss.
secondaryObservations.proposedFollowUp: Separate finding with its own 3x repetition. Candidate direction, NOT applied here: pair the FINAL CHECK with a symmetric positive check ('...and confirm every OTHER key the rules require for that step — including Rule 6's `headers` — is still present') and add a guard that a name the user spoke is never flagged. Also add a tier-0 criterion for 'no opaque ID in missing_parameters' to catch (b) and (c), which currently pass silently.
secondaryObservations.doNotBundle: Keep out of remedy 1 so the srw-02/ctfm-03 A/B stays attributable to a single Rule 6 change.

secondaryObservations.priority: HIGH — settle before or alongside shipping remedy 1
secondaryObservations.observation: The model's behaviour may be substantively RIGHT even though it is spec-noncompliant, and the codebase contradicts itself on the point. composio_engine.py:244-264 states 'Unmatched keys pass through unchanged', and `headers` is never consumed by name anywhere in the backend, so a `headers` key on AIRTABLE_CREATE_RECORD is forwarded to Composio rather than dropped — where Airtable's real schema has no headers concept, because a `fields` object names its own columns. Meanwhile tier0_code_checks.py:92-112 articulates exactly that principle in its own comment ('the payload is KEY-ADDRESSED and already names its own columns') but applies the exemption to Notion `properties` and NOT to Airtable `fields`, which is equally key-addressed. So the criterion demands on Airtable precisely what its own stated rationale would exempt.
secondaryObservations.whyItStillWarrantsRemedy1: Every declared source of intent requires headers here — agentspec.yaml:44, :199 and :235, the srw-02 and fan-01 seed rationales, Rule 6's explicit naming of Airtable, and the Phase-3 baseline in which all three Airtable writes carried headers with no reported execution failures. Restoring the specified, previously-observed behaviour is the correct default; changing the spec is a deliberate decision the operator should make explicitly, not a silent drift.
secondaryObservations.proposedFollowUp: Before or immediately after remedy 1, execute one real AIRTABLE_CREATE_RECORD through composio_engine with and without a `headers` key and record whether Composio rejects the extra property, ignores it, or uses it. If it is rejected or harmful, take remedy 2 INSTEAD of remedy 1 and update agentspec.yaml:44/:199/:235 to match; if it is ignored or useful, ship remedy 1 as written.

secondaryObservations.observation: 28320b1 embedded amb-02's seed prompt VERBATIM into planner.py:33 ('Grab the latest orders from our internal API and drop them into one of my spreadsheets'), together with its correct answer. amb-02's post-optimize step-2 key set is now `[row_data, headers]`, a character-for-character match to that exemplar. amb-02 has therefore stopped being a held-out measurement of generalization and become a memorization check, which is likely part of why the amb-02 fix looked so clean while srw-02 silently broke.
secondaryObservations.mitigationAppliedHere: Remedy 1's worked example deliberately uses tokens absent from the entire dataset and both trace files — 'Ops Budget', 'Q3 Spend', 'Northgate Supply' each verified at 0 occurrences in eval-dataset-candidates.json and traces/*.jsonl — and names a base AND table so it never demonstrates the missing-parameter decision that srw-02 tests. srw-02 therefore remains a clean held-out measurement of remedy 1.
secondaryObservations.proposedFollowUp: Adopt as a standing convention for this optimize loop: worked examples in the system prompt must use tokens that appear in no eval seed, and any exemplar reusing a seed prompt retires that seed from the scorecard.

remedies.title: Rescope Rule 6 by ACTION SHAPE rather than row-positional vocabulary, and give it its own worked Airtable-with-headers example
remedies.targetLocation: get_system_prompt(), Rule 6 — replace line 56 in full (single line -> four lines). No other line is touched.
remedies.whyThisSiteNotRule2: The dispatch asked whether the cleaner fix is Rule 6 or Rule 2's FINAL CHECK. The evidence settles it rather than leaving it to taste. (1) REACHABILITY: ctfm-03 exhibits the defect with `missing_parameters: []`, so Rule 2's block is never entered and its FINAL CHECK loop iterates zero times — no Rule 2 edit can reach that trace, which alone disqualifies Rule 2 as the fix site. (2) SPECIFICITY: Rule 6 is the rule actually being violated and its scope clause is where the omission is licensed; Rule 2 is not violated by these traces at all — srw-02's handling of `table_name` is exactly right and must not be disturbed. (3) BLAST RADIUS: git diff 0639887..HEAD shows Rule 6 is byte-for-byte untouched by all four shipped fixes, so editing it has zero textual overlap with any of them, whereas Rule 2's FINAL CHECK is the newest and most load-bearing text in the prompt — amb-02, amb-01, amb-03, ctfm-01 and msh-03 all now depend on it, and it is the same text implicated in the S1 over-pruning regressions. Rewording it would put four shipped fixes and this one on a single non-attributable A/B.
remedies.rationale: Rule 6 already commands headers on Airtable and the model is not defying it — it is applying the rule's own stated reasoning correctly. Rule 6 scopes itself with positional-row vocabulary ('writes row(s)', 'alongside the row data', 'in the same order as `headers`') and justifies itself with a strictly positional mechanism ('tools otherwise treat the very first row of data as the column headers'), none of which engages an Airtable `fields` object whose keys already are the column names; and it names only two triggering shapes, both cross-references to Rule 5 and Rule 3, neither of which srw-02 or ctfm-03 invokes. Meanwhile the only worked Airtable `parameters` object anywhere in the prompt (planner.py:53) lists `base_name` and nothing else. The failing output is that exemplar's key set plus the payload, on the one shape Rule 6 forgot to name. This remedy removes the model's discretion about whether a given write 'counts' and gives Rule 6 the two properties diagnose-finding-5 established are what make a rule stick here: a point-of-use statement and a worked example.
remedies.whyWorks: Four mechanisms, each closing one link in the why-chain. (1) The scope clause is restated as an ACTION-SHAPE test naming the exact verb list the criterion gates on (ADD_ROW / APPEND_ROW / INSERT_ROW / CREATE_ROW / ADD_RECORD / CREATE_RECORD / BATCH_UPDATE), so applicability is decided by the action slug the model has already chosen rather than by an inference about whether the payload is positional — AIRTABLE_CREATE_RECORD matches on its face. (2) A third triggering shape, 'a single record whose field values the user gave directly in their own request', is added to the appositive, naming precisely the shape srw-02 and ctfm-03 are and that the two-item enumeration silently excluded. (3) The first new bullet decouples the requirement from the payload's name and internal structure and states explicitly that key-addressed keys do not satisfy it, then supplies the prompt's first Airtable `parameters` object containing `headers` — directly counterweighting the headerless exemplar at planner.py:53, at the point of use, in the same delivery form that made the Rule 5 carve-out stick on fan-01. (4) The third new bullet forecloses the missing_parameters interaction as an aggravating factor (srw-02 fails 3/3 with a flagged key while ctfm-03 fails 2/3 without one, which is consistent with it aggravating even though it does not cause), and it does so as a general principle — omitting a flagged key never licenses omitting anything else — that also hardens the step body against the S1 over-pruning pressure without touching Rule 2's text.
remedies.regressionSafety: The Notion exception bullet is written to match tier0_code_checks.py:104-112 exactly: the criterion exempts a non-empty `properties` dict, and so does the new bullet, so ctfm-01 and msh-03 (Notion page creation, currently scored n/a) cannot be pushed into emitting a spurious headers key. The verb list is copied from POSITIONAL_ROW_VERBS at tier0_code_checks.py:98-101, so prompt and criterion agree by construction rather than by coincidence. The worked example names both `base_name` AND `table_name`, so it never demonstrates the flag-vs-literal decision and cannot re-teach srw-02's or fan-01's answer. Its tokens ('Ops Budget', 'Q3 Spend', 'Northgate Supply') were each verified at zero occurrences across eval-dataset-candidates.json and both trace files, so no eval seed is contaminated.

diff.before: Rule 6 (Headers for Spreadsheet/Table Row Writes): Whenever a step writes row(s) of structured data into a spreadsheet/table/database (Google Sheets, Airtable, a Notion database, ...) — whether it's a Rule 5 fan-out (many rows) or a single record (e.g. one row of extracted fields from Rule 3, such as name/email/company) — ALWAYS also include a `headers` parameter alongside the row data: a short list of column-name strings, one per field/column being written (e.g. `["Caption"]` for one column, or `["Name", "Email", "Company"]` for a multi-field record). Many of these tools otherwise treat the very first row of data as the column headers instead of storing it, silently discarding what should have been real data — this is true even for a SINGLE row, which would otherwise be entirely lost. When writing one structured record with multiple fields, reference the WHOLE extraction result as the row-data placeholder (e.g. `{{{{step_N_result}}}}`) rather than trying to pull individual fields out yourself — the execution engine turns a single JSON object into one row with one cell per field, in the same order as `headers`.
diff.after:
Rule 6 (Headers for Spreadsheet/Table Row Writes): Whenever a step appends a row or creates a record in a spreadsheet/table/database (Google Sheets, Airtable, a Notion database, ...) — i.e. any action of the shape ADD_ROW / APPEND_ROW / INSERT_ROW / CREATE_ROW / ADD_RECORD / CREATE_RECORD / BATCH_UPDATE, and whether it's a Rule 5 fan-out (many rows), a single record of fields an earlier step extracted under Rule 3 (such as name/email/company), or a single record whose field values the user gave directly in their own request — ALWAYS also include a `headers` parameter alongside the row data: a short list of column-name strings, one per field/column being written (e.g. `["Caption"]` for one column, or `["Name", "Email", "Company"]` for a multi-field record). Many of these tools otherwise treat the very first row of data as the column headers instead of storing it, silently discarding what should have been real data — this is true even for a SINGLE row, which would otherwise be entirely lost. When writing one structured record with multiple fields, reference the WHOLE extraction result as the row-data placeholder (e.g. `{{{{step_N_result}}}}`) rather than trying to pull individual fields out yourself — the execution engine turns a single JSON object into one row with one cell per field, in the same order as `headers`.
- Whether `headers` is required is decided by that ACTION SHAPE alone — never by what you happen to name the payload parameter, and never by how that payload is structured internally. `row_data`, `values`, `record_data` and an Airtable `fields` object are all the same case: `headers` is a separate sibling key in the same `parameters` object and is still required alongside it. A payload whose KEYS already read like column names does NOT remove the requirement — still emit `headers` listing those same columns in the same order. Worked Airtable example — "add this expense to my Airtable base Ops Budget, Q3 Spend table: vendor Northgate Supply, amount 850, category Software": `parameters` is `{{"base_name": "Ops Budget", "table_name": "Q3 Spend", "fields": {{"Vendor": "Northgate Supply", "Amount": 850, "Category": "Software"}}, "headers": ["Vendor", "Amount", "Category"]}}`.
- The one exception is creating a Notion PAGE (e.g. NOTION_CREATE_PAGE, NOTION_CREATE_DATABASE_PAGE) whose content is a `properties` object — that is not a positional row append, so it needs no `headers`.
- `headers` is never optional, and it is never dropped to make a step look smaller or more "incomplete". If this step also carries a `missing_parameters` entry, leaving that one flagged key out under Rule 2 does NOT license leaving anything else out: every other rule, this one included, still applies in full to the rest of the step body. A step is meant to be incomplete in exactly the flagged key and complete in every other respect.

remedies.escapingNote: CRITICAL — get_system_prompt() returns an f-string, so every literal brace in the `after` text is DOUBLED in source and renders single. Source `{{"base_name": "Ops Budget", ..., "fields": {{"Vendor": ...}}, "headers": [...]}}` renders to single braces. The existing `{{{{step_N_result}}}}` (four braces) is preserved verbatim and renders to `{{step_N_result}}` (two braces) — that is Rule 6's pre-existing convention and is deliberately left alone; do NOT 'normalise' it as part of this change. The `after` text is the PLANNER.PY SOURCE form and must be pasted exactly as-is. Verified by evaluating it as an f-string and asserting equality with the agentspec mirror.

remedies.title: Alternative if S2 resolves the other way — exempt key-addressed payloads in the criterion instead of forcing headers in the prompt
remedies.rationale: tier0_code_checks.py:92-97 states the governing principle in its own words — the pathology Rule 6 prevents 'cannot occur when ... the payload is KEY-ADDRESSED and already names its own columns' — and then applies the exemption to Notion `properties` (line 109-111) but not to Airtable `fields`, which is equally key-addressed. If the S2 execution test shows Composio rejects or mishandles an extra `headers` property on AIRTABLE_CREATE_RECORD, then the model's behaviour is substantively correct and it is the criterion, not the planner, that is inconsistent with its own stated rationale.
remedies.whyWorks: Extending the key-addressed exemption from `properties` to any dict-valued payload under a `fields`/`properties`/`record` key makes the check test the pathology it was written to test — positional row appends — instead of penalising a payload shape that cannot exhibit it. It would move srw-02 and ctfm-03 from fail to n/a on grounds the check itself already endorses, rather than by weakening the bar.
remedies.describedChange: In _is_positional_row_write (tier0_code_checks.py:104-112), generalise the key-addressed exemption: instead of inspecting only params.get('properties'), iterate a tuple of payload key names ('properties', 'fields', 'record', 'record_data') and return False if any of them holds a non-empty dict, keeping the existing comment's rationale. Then update the three intent statements that would become stale — agentspec.yaml:44 (SOP description), :199 (criterion description) and :235 (expectedBehavior 'Includes a headers parameter matching the row data's fields, whether it's one row or a fan-out batch') — to say the requirement applies to positional row appends and not to key-addressed record payloads. Rule 6 in planner.py and agentspec.yaml would then need the same carve-out stated positively so the planner is not being scored against a rule the prompt still asserts. This is a SPEC CHANGE and should be an explicit operator decision, not a silent drift; it is mutually exclusive with remedy 1.
remedies.cost_note: Cheap to implement, but it retires srw-02's stated purpose ('extends the header-safety requirement past Google Sheets to a table/database target'), so the seed should be rewritten or removed rather than left scoring n/a.
applyInstructions: 1. Do NOT apply speculatively. Run the S2 test first: execute one real AIRTABLE_CREATE_RECORD through composio_engine.execute_composio_action with and without a `headers` key and record whether Composio rejects the extra property, silently ignores it, or uses it.
2. If Composio ignores or uses it, DISCARD this remedy and ship remedy 1 unchanged.

3. If Composio rejects it (or it corrupts the record), apply this remedy INSTEAD of remedy 1: generalise the exemption in _is_positional_row_write, update agentspec.yaml:44/:199/:235, and add the matching carve-out to Rule 6 in both planner.py:56 and agentspec.yaml:138.
4. Rewrite or retire the srw-02 seed, whose entire stated purpose is the requirement this remedy removes.
5. Re-run the full 24-trace regression and confirm fan-01 (Airtable fan-out, currently emitting headers) is scored consistently under the new rule.

remedies.title: Close the two harness gaps that let this regression ship — single-run sampling and seed-prompt contamination
remedies.rationale: This regression reached main because the harness cannot see it. traces/planner-eval-traces-post-optimize.jsonl holds exactly ONE run per trace_id, so ctfm-03's 2-in-3 defect had a one-in-three chance of being recorded clean, and the four non-failing row-write traces in this finding rest on n=1 each. The identical limitation was raised as remedy 3 of diagnose-finding-5-amb02.json and was not adopted, and the very next promotion shipped two regressions. Separately, 28320b1 embedded amb-02's seed prompt verbatim into planner.py:33 with its answer, so amb-02 now measures memorization rather than generalization.
remedies.whyWorks: Repeating each seed N times and failing a criterion if ANY repetition contradicts converts a sampled observation into a bound, and reporting k/N incidence makes a partial defect like ctfm-03's visible instead of a coin flip. A contamination lint makes the S3 failure mode impossible to reintroduce silently, at zero runtime cost.
remedies.describedChange: (a) Add a `--repeat N` flag to run_dataset_through_planner.py (default 1; use 3 at minimum for the spreadsheet-row-write, fan-out-batch, cross-tool-field-mismatch and ambiguous-recipient-or-target scenarios), tagging each emitted trace with metadata.repetition. (b) In tier0_code_checks.py, aggregate verdicts across repetitions of the same trace_id base and return fail if ANY repetition fails, reporting the k/N incidence in the note — apply this to check_sheet_header_safety at minimum. (c) Add a standalone lint that reads eval-dataset-candidates.json and get_system_prompt() and fails if any seed's prompt_text, or a distinctive substring of it, appears verbatim in the system prompt; run it in the same gate as the tier-0 checks. (d) Add a criterion asserting no entry in missing_parameters has an opaque-ID-shaped parameter_key (matching planner.py:39), which would currently catch amb-01's `channel_id` and msh-03's `parent_page_id` from S1.
applyInstructions: 1. Add `--repeat N` to run_dataset_through_planner.py, tagging each trace with metadata.repetition.
2. Group verdicts by trace_id base in tier0_code_checks.py and fail if any repetition fails; surface k/N in the note.
3. Re-baseline BEFORE applying remedy 1 so the pre-fix incidence (expected 3/3 srw-02, 2/3 ctfm-03) is on record, then re-run after so the A/B is a like-for-like comparison.
4. Add the contamination lint (c) and the opaque-ID criterion (d); expect (c) to fail immediately on amb-02 and (d) on amb-01 and msh-03, which is the point.
5. Extend repetition to fan-01, srw-01, srw-03, amb-02 and ctfm-01 so the four already-shipped fixes finally get the determinism bound they were never held to.
assumptions: The harness scripts are editable and re-runnable in this environment; tier0_code_checks.py was read directly, run_dataset_through_planner.py and aggregate_scorecard.py were located but not executed.
Three repetitions suffice to catch a ~2/3-incidence defect with acceptable confidence; a genuinely rare (<10%) residual would still slip through.
Extra Gemini spend from repetition is acceptable when scoped to the four listed scenarios rather than all 24 seeds.
